content: Chest pain with shortness of breath, sweating, or radiation to the arm/jaw is a medical emergency. Patients should call 911 immediately. Aspirin 325mg should be chewed if not allergic. Time is muscle — every minute of delay increases myocardial damage. Door-to-balloon time target is under 90 minutes for STEMI.

Stable angina presents as chest tightness triggered by exertion, relieved by rest or nitroglycerin within 5 minutes. Unstable angina occurs at rest or is increasing in frequency — requires immediate emergency evaluation. Patients with coronary artery disease reporting new chest pain should be treated as emergency. Nitroglycerin sublingual may be used every 5 minutes up to 3 doses.

CAD management requires antiplatelet therapy, statins, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and beta-blockers. LDL target below 70 mg/dL for high-risk patients. Aspirin contraindication requires alternative antiplatelet. Post-CABG patients require lifelong anticoagulation assessment. Annual cardiology follow-up recommended. Warfarin INR target 2.0-3.0 for post-CABG patients.

STEMI requires immediate reperfusion via primary PCI within 90 minutes. If PCI unavailable, fibrinolysis within 30 minutes. Dual antiplatelet therapy required. NSAIDs increase cardiovascular events post-MI and are contraindicated. Beta-blockers reduce mortality. ACE inhibitors improve outcomes especially with reduced EF.

Heart failure management requires four pillars: ACE inhibitor or ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor. Sodium restriction below 2g/day. Daily weight monitoring — gain of 2-3 pounds in 24 hours indicates fluid retention requiring urgent attention. Avoid NSAIDs as they cause sodium retention and worsen heart failure. Fluid restriction 1.5L/day for advanced HF.

Acute HF decompensation signs: sudden weight gain above 2kg in 24 hours, worsening dyspnea especially lying flat, leg and ankle edema, fatigue, elevated JVP. These require urgent or emergency evaluation. BNP above 400 pg/mL confirms decompensation. IV diuretics and oxygen required. ICU admission if hemodynamic instability.

topic: heart failure reduced ejection fraction treatment
content: HFrEF defined as EF below 40%. Guideline-directed medical therapy requires sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI) preferred over ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker titrated to maximum tolerated dose, spironolactone or eplerenone for MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor. ICD indicated for EF persistently below 35% despite optimal therapy. CRT for LBBB with QRS above 150ms.

Digoxin in heart failure: narrow therapeutic index 0.5-0.9 ng/mL for HF. Toxicity causes nausea, vomiting, visual halos, bradycardia, arrhythmias. Hypokalemia from diuretics dramatically increases digoxin toxicity risk — monitor potassium closely. Amiodarone and verapamil increase digoxin levels by 50-100%. Reduce dose in CKD. Monthly level monitoring recommended.

Hypertension defined as BP consistently above 130/80 mmHg. Stage 2 HTN requires medication plus lifestyle. First-line agents: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazide diuretics, calcium channel blockers. Target below 130/80 for diabetes, CKD, and high cardiovascular risk. Hypertensive urgency above 180/120 mmHg without organ damage: oral therapy, monitor 1-2 hours.

Hypertensive crisis: BP above 180/120 mmHg. Emergency if end-organ damage present (chest pain, stroke, pulmonary edema, AKI). Requires IV labetalol or nicardipine. Reduce MAP by maximum 25% in first hour — too rapid reduction causes ischemia. Urgency without organ damage: oral amlodipine or labetalol. Do not use sublingual nifedipine — dangerous rapid drop.

T2DM management: HbA1c target below 7% for most adults, 7-8% acceptable for elderly or complex patients. Metformin is first-line unless contraindicated. Add SGLT2 inhibitor for cardiovascular disease or HF. Add GLP-1 agonist for obesity or CV risk reduction. Annual eye exams, foot exams, kidney function and lipid panels. BP below 130/80 mmHg. Statin therapy for all T2DM above age 40.

Diabetes complications include neuropathy, nephropathy, retinopathy, and cardiovascular disease. HbA1c every 3 months if not at goal, every 6 months if stable. DKA symptoms: excessive thirst, nausea, abdominal pain, fruity breath, blood glucose above 250 mg/dL — requires emergency care. Monofilament foot exam annually. Urine albumin-creatinine ratio annually.

Metformin contraindicated when eGFR below 30 mL/min. Dose reduction required for eGFR 30-45 — maximum 1000mg/day. Must be held 48 hours before iodinated contrast procedures due to lactic acidosis risk. Resume only after confirming stable renal function post-procedure. Alcohol use increases lactic acidosis risk. Most effective, safest, and cheapest T2DM medication. Does not cause hypoglycemia.

SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) recommended for T2DM with established CVD, HF, or CKD. Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin reduce HF hospitalizations in HFrEF regardless of diabetes. Reduce dose in CKD — check eGFR before starting. Hold before surgery. Risk of genital mycotic infections and DKA. Check for amputation risk before use.

GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide) recommended for T2DM with obesity or established CVD. Semaglutide 2.4mg weekly significantly reduces body weight. Common side effects: nausea, vomiting — start at low dose and titrate. Contraindicated with personal or family history of MTC or MEN2. Do not use with severe GI disease.

Basal insulin (glargine, detemir) started at 10 units or 0.1-0.2 units/kg at bedtime. Titrate by 2 units every 3 days until fasting glucose below 130 mg/dL. During illness, stress, or infection — insulin requirements increase significantly. Monitor glucose every 2-4 hours during acute illness. Never stop insulin in T1DM. DKA risk if insulin omitted in T1DM.

CKD management: BP below 130/80 mmHg, ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria above 300mg/day, avoid nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast without hydration). Monitor eGFR, potassium, phosphorus, hemoglobin regularly. Metformin dose adjustment when eGFR 30-45, stop when below 30. Contrast agents require pre-hydration with IV saline. Avoid NSAID use in any stage of CKD.

CKD requires drug dose adjustments: Metformin — reduce at eGFR 30-45, stop below 30. Digoxin — reduce dose, risk of toxicity increases. Lisinopril — safe but monitor potassium and creatinine. Furosemide — may need higher doses. NSAIDs absolutely contraindicated — worsen CKD and cause AKI. Spironolactone — use with extreme caution below eGFR 45, hold if potassium above 5.0.

Hyperkalemia in CKD: potassium above 5.5 mEq/L requires intervention. Potassium above 6.0 with ECG changes is emergency. Avoid potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors may need dose reduction. Dietary potassium restriction below 2g/day. Patiromer or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate for chronic management. In acute hyperkalemia: calcium gluconate for cardiac protection, insulin-dextrose to shift K+ intracellularly.

Warfarin HIGH RISK interactions: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin) significantly increase bleeding risk — contraindicated combination. Antibiotics (metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, azithromycin) increase warfarin effect — reduce dose and monitor INR closely. Amiodarone dramatically increases warfarin effect. INR must be monitored within 3-5 days of any medication change. Supratherapeutic INR above 4.0 increases hemorrhage risk significantly.

Warfarin therapeutic ranges: INR 2.0-3.0 for AF, DVT/PE. INR 2.5-3.5 for mechanical aortic valve. Sub-therapeutic INR increases clot risk. Supratherapeutic INR above 4.0 — hold warfarin, vitamin K if bleeding. INR above 10 — emergency reversal with IV vitamin K and 4-factor PCC. Fresh foods high in vitamin K (leafy greens) reduce warfarin effect. Consistent diet important.

NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac) contraindicated in: heart failure (cause sodium retention and decompensation), CKD any stage (cause AKI), anticoagulation/warfarin (increase bleeding risk), post-MI (increase cardiovascular events), peptic ulcer disease. Use acetaminophen as alternative. If NSAID required, use shortest duration and lowest dose with proton pump inhibitor.

Digoxin narrow therapeutic index 0.5-2.0 ng/mL; use 0.5-0.9 for HF. Toxicity signs: nausea, vomiting, yellow-green visual halos, bradycardia, any arrhythmia, confusion. Hypokalemia from diuretics increases digoxin toxicity dramatically — even therapeutic levels become toxic when K+ below 3.5. Amiodarone and verapamil increase digoxin concentration by 50-100% — halve dose when adding.

Metformin must be held 48 hours before iodinated contrast procedures (CT scan with contrast, cardiac cath, angiography). Resume only after confirming stable renal function 48 hours post-procedure. Iodinated contrast can cause acute kidney injury, which reduces metformin clearance causing dangerous lactic acidosis. Risk highest with eGFR below 60, dehydration, large contrast volume.

Penicillin allergy: 1-10% cross-reactivity with cephalosporins. True anaphylaxis to penicillin requires avoidance of all beta-lactams unless allergist-supervised challenge. Azithromycin, clindamycin, or vancomycin as alternatives for gram-positive infections. Carbapenems (meropenem, imipenem) have very low cross-reactivity — can usually be used with monitoring. Many patients labeled penicillin-allergic are not truly allergic — allergy testing recommended.

ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril) can cause angioedema — potentially life-threatening. Discontinue immediately and use ARB as alternative. Monitor potassium and creatinine within 1-2 weeks of starting. Expected creatinine rise up to 30% acceptable. Avoid in pregnancy — teratogenic. Cough in 10-15% of patients — switch to ARB. Avoid combining ACE inhibitor with ARB.

Statins: monitor for myopathy (muscle pain, weakness). Rhabdomyolysis rare but serious — CK above 10x ULN requires stopping statin. High-intensity statins (atorvastatin 40-80mg, rosuvastatin 20-40mg) for very high cardiovascular risk. Drug interactions: amiodarone, cyclosporine increase statin levels and myopathy risk. Simvastatin 80mg should not be started due to high myopathy risk.

FAST acronym: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 911. Other symptoms: sudden severe headache, vision loss, dizziness, unilateral numbness. tPA must be given within 4.5 hours of onset — call 911 immediately. Do not give aspirin until CT confirms no hemorrhage. Time is brain — 1.9 million neurons die per minute. Thrombectomy up to 24 hours for selected patients.

Secondary stroke prevention in AFib requires anticoagulation — warfarin INR 2-3 or DOAC (apixaban preferred). Antiplatelet therapy insufficient for cardioembolic stroke from AFib. BP target below 130/80 — most important modifiable risk factor. High-intensity statin for all ischemic stroke with LDL below 70. Avoid NSAIDs post-stroke — increase cardiovascular events.

Sepsis: life-threatening organ dysfunction from dysregulated infection response. Signs: fever above 38.3C or hypothermia below 36C, HR above 90, RR above 20, altered mental status, WBC above 12000 or below 4000. Septic shock: persistent hypotension despite 30mL/kg IV fluids with lactate above 2 mmol/L. Requires IV antibiotics within 1 HOUR, blood cultures before antibiotics, IV fluids 30mL/kg.

Septic shock management: norepinephrine first-line vasopressor, target MAP above 65 mmHg. Add vasopressin if norepinephrine above 0.25 mcg/kg/min. Hydrocortisone 200mg/day if vasopressor-dependent. Tight glucose control 140-180 mg/dL using insulin infusion. Lactate clearance monitoring every 2 hours. Duration antibiotics typically 7-10 days. Procalcitonin guides antibiotic de-escalation.

Asthma management: inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are cornerstone controller therapy. Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin in NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease. Rescue inhaler (albuterol) for acute symptoms — use more than 2x per week indicates poor control. Moderate persistent asthma: ICS-LABA combination. Severe attack: SpO2 below 92%, inability to complete sentences — emergency care required.

Acute asthma exacerbation: continuous nebulized albuterol, ipratropium, systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 40-60mg), supplemental oxygen to SpO2 above 94%. Severe: IV magnesium sulfate 2g over 20 minutes. Peak flow below 50% predicted is severe. PEFR monitoring every 20 minutes. Discharge criteria: PEF above 70%, SpO2 above 94% on room air.

topic: NSAID aspirin exacerbated respiratory disease asthma
content: NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD): aspirin and NSAIDs cause severe bronchospasm in 10-20% of adult asthmatics. Avoid all NSAIDs and COX-1 inhibitors. Use acetaminophen for pain (generally safe below 1g/dose). COX-2 selective agents (celecoxib) generally tolerated with caution. If NSAID absolutely required, aspirin desensitization protocol under specialist supervision.

AFib stroke prevention: CHA2DS2-VASc score guides anticoagulation. Score 2+ in men — anticoagulation recommended. Warfarin INR 2-3 or DOAC (apixaban preferred — fewer bleeds). Aspirin NOT recommended as stroke prevention in AFib — insufficient and bleeds. Rate control target HR below 110 at rest. Anticoagulate 3 weeks before cardioversion or use TEE to exclude clot.

AFib rate control: beta-blockers (metoprolol, carvedilol) or calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil). Digoxin as adjunct — less effective for exercise-related rate control. Target resting HR below 80 or lenient control below 110 in asymptomatic patients. Avoid digoxin in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. Avoid verapamil in HFrEF — negative inotrope.

Anaphylaxis: epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) 0.3mg IM into outer thigh is FIRST-LINE — inject immediately, call 911. Second dose after 5-15 minutes if no improvement. Antihistamines (diphenhydramine) are adjunct ONLY — never primary treatment. Corticosteroids prevent biphasic reactions. Patient must be observed 4-6 hours after reaction. Prescribe epinephrine auto-injector and action plan.

BNP above 100 pg/mL suggests heart failure; above 400 pg/mL likely decompensated HF. Troponin elevation indicates myocardial injury. Serial troponin every 3 hours for ACS rule-in/rule-out. Digoxin level: therapeutic 0.5-0.9 ng/mL for HF. INR: therapeutic 2.0-3.0 for AF/DVT. Potassium monitoring critical for patients on digoxin, diuretics, ACE inhibitors, or spironolactone.

COPD exacerbation: increased dyspnea, cough, sputum. Treat with SABA plus SAMA nebulization, systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 40mg x5 days), antibiotics if purulent sputum or CXR infiltrate. SpO2 target 88-92% — avoid hyperoxia which causes CO2 retention. NIV (BiPAP) for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure. Long-term: tiotropium (LAMA) plus ICS-LABA for frequent exacerbators.

DVT/PE treatment: anticoagulate immediately. DOAC (rivaroxaban, apixaban) preferred over warfarin for most patients. Warfarin if DOAC contraindicated (severe CKD, antiphospholipid syndrome) — INR 2-3. Duration: provoked DVT 3 months; unprovoked or PE 6 months or indefinite. Massive PE with hemodynamic instability: thrombolysis. Compression stockings for DVT.

DKA criteria: glucose above 250 mg/dL, pH below 7.3, bicarbonate below 15, ketonemia. Signs: polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath, altered mental status. Treatment: IV insulin infusion, aggressive IV fluids, potassium replacement, monitor glucose hourly. Continue insulin until anion gap closed. Never stop insulin in T1DM even when not eating.

topic: medications to avoid in elderly patients
content: Beers Criteria: avoid in elderly (65+): NSAIDs (GI bleed, AKI, fluid retention), benzodiazepines (fall risk, delirium), anticholinergics (confusion, urinary retention), nitrofurantoin below eGFR 45. Use lowest effective doses. Review polypharmacy — patients on 5+ medications have high risk of drug interactions. Digoxin above 0.125mg daily increases toxicity risk in elderly.

Fall risk medications: antihypertensives (orthostatic hypotension), diuretics (volume depletion), benzodiazepines and sedatives, opioids, antidepressants, antipsychotics. Assess orthostatic BP in all elderly hypertensive patients — drop of 20/10 mmHg on standing indicates risk. Exercise programs (strength and balance) most effective for fall prevention. Vitamin D 800 IU daily reduces falls.

CRITICAL drug interaction pairs: (1) Warfarin + NSAIDs = major bleeding risk; (2) ACE inhibitor + potassium-sparing diuretic = hyperkalemia; (3) Digoxin + amiodarone = digoxin toxicity, halve digoxin dose; (4) Metformin + contrast dye = lactic acidosis, hold 48h; (5) Statin + amiodarone = myopathy risk; (6) Warfarin + azithromycin = INR elevation; (7) NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic = triple whammy AKI.

Anticoagulant safety: Never combine warfarin with NSAIDs without very close INR monitoring. DOAC with NSAIDs: increased GI bleeding. All anticoagulants contraindicated with active bleeding. Before surgery: hold warfarin 5 days (INR below 1.5). Bridge with heparin if high thromboembolic risk. Warfarin reversal: vitamin K plus 4-factor PCC for emergency. Fish oil and vitamin E also increase bleeding risk.

Platinum compound hypersensitivity (carboplatin, cisplatin, oxaliplatin) is a contraindication to platinum-based chemotherapy. Patients with documented platinum allergy should receive alternative regimens. In breast cancer, consider taxane-based (paclitaxel, docetaxel) or anthracycline-based (doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide) regimens as alternatives. Cross-reactivity between platinum agents is common — prior reaction to one agent contraindicates all platinum compounds.

Standard chemotherapy regimens for breast cancer: AC-T (doxorubicin + cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel) for HER2-negative disease. Trastuzumab-based for HER2-positive. Tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors for hormone receptor-positive disease. Platinum-based regimens considered for triple-negative breast cancer or BRCA-mutated tumours. Multidisciplinary tumour board review recommended for complex cases.

Drug allergies in oncology require immediate documentation and consideration of alternative agents. High criticality allergies are absolute contraindications. Oncology MDT review is mandatory before proceeding with any alternative regimen in a patient with documented chemotherapy allergy. All allergy information must be documented as a FHIR AllergyIntolerance resource with criticality level.

topic: breast cancer tumour board referral MDT
content: Multidisciplinary tumour board (MDT) review is recommended for breast cancer patients with drug allergies to standard chemotherapy agents. MDT should include medical oncology, surgical oncology, radiation oncology, and pathology. ServiceRequest for MDT referral should be created with priority URGENT when treatment-limiting allergies are identified.

topic: tamoxifen drug interactions breast cancer hormonal therapy
content: Tamoxifen interactions: avoid strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine) as they reduce tamoxifen efficacy. Warfarin interaction — tamoxifen potentiates anticoagulant effect, INR monitoring required. Tamoxifen increases risk of thromboembolic events — assess VTE risk before initiation. Duration 5-10 years for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer. Safe with Metformin in T2DM patients.
